analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal approval of oil and gas drilling permits, auto-issuing them if decisions lag.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Mineral Leasing Act to require the Interior Department to decide on drilling permit applications for certain federal oil and gas leases within 90 days. If the Department misses the deadline without acting, the permit would automatically be considered issued. It would also require a report on the backlog of permit applications on federal land.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases with pending permit applications. They would get a decision within 90 days of a complete application, and if the Interior Department missed that window without approving or formally deferring the permit, it would be considered issued automatically. A required report on the permitting backlog would also give the industry a documented case for further statutory easing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies with federal leases

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Interior Secretary to issue a decision on a qualifying drilling permit application within 90 days of a complete application, if the Secretary has not already issued or deferred it within an initial 30-day period.
If the Secretary misses the 90-day deadline without deciding, the permit is automatically considered issued, removing the agency's ability to hold it open.

The bill directs the Bureau of Land Management to report within 180 days on the size of the drilling permit backlog, its causes, and recommendations for clearing it, including requests for financial or statutory help from Congress.

analysis.who_pays: The general public, in the form of reduced federal oversight: drilling on public land could move forward without a completed agency decision when deadlines are missed, and the Interior Department would lose its ability to defer permits pending review. Communities and conservation interests concerned about drilling on federal land bear the environmental and land-use effects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal oversight of drilling on public land

drawbacks.text: Automatic issuance would let a drilling permit take effect without any agency decision at all once the 90-day window lapses, so drilling could proceed with no completed federal determination on that permit.

The mandatory deadlines and auto-approval strip the Interior Department of the discretion the Mineral Leasing Act otherwise gives it to defer permits, including deferral where an applicant has required steps outstanding — narrowing the government's ability to pause drilling on public land.

For a supporter, the honest cost is speed over review: shorter agency timelines and self-executing permits trade federal vetting of public-land drilling for faster permit turnaround, and the bill offers nothing on reclaiming funds for oversold but undeveloped federal leases or on the fiscal terms of existing leases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted easing of federal drilling rules whose main beneficiaries are oil and gas companies operating on federal leases; its potential benefit to the public — more rapid domestic production — is not established in the record, while the cost is concrete: permits auto-issued without a decision and a narrowed ability to defer drilling on public land. On the evidence provided, the costs fall on public oversight and the gains on the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Budd (R-NC) introduced the Unleash American Drilling Act on June 22, 2022, joined by nine Republican cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken.
The bill expired at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much: the oil and gas industry got no new permitting rights, and federal agencies kept their existing discretion over drilling permits. The bill's death left the status quo intact rather than changing who benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies kept existing permit discretion

for.name: Rep. Ted Budd
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose 90-day deadlines and automatic issuance on federal drilling permits.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 22, 2022, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten initial sponsors — Rep. Budd and nine cosponsors — were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled committee never advanced the bill, and no Democrat sponsored it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with federal leases
industries.note: The bill would speed permit decisions on their federal leases and auto-issue permits the Department fails to decide in 90 days, reducing federal review of drilling on public land. The benefit flows to leaseholders; the offsetting cost is reduced oversight of public-land drilling, which the public bears.

industries.industry: Federal land conservation and oversight interests
industries.note: Auto-issued permits and narrowed deferral authority would remove tools used to pause drilling pending review, weakening the public's ability to oversee extraction on federal land.
